name: Beth Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't campaign for anything. Everything's confidential, so you can tell me the public version and the private one. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the new connections crew for the electricity company in Brookfield, which is a commuter town that's doubled in fifteen years. So it's new estates mostly: running the service cable from the street to each house, fitting the cut-out, the main fuse box where the power comes in. More and more it's upgrades for car chargers and heat pumps, people wanting a bigger supply.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the variety and I like a tidy job, all the labels right, the paperwork done. What's hard is the pace, because the builders want ten houses a day and the office wants them done safely, and those two things fight. And money's tight; Sam drives a delivery van and between us we're always about a fortnight from the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that seems plausible enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say fair enough, the useful bits stay and the rest goes quiet. I'd probably post a joke in the crew group chat about the tablets still not working in the rain. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief for both of us, because Sam's job would have been in the firing line too. But it doesn't fix the money. We'd still be a fortnight from the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal. I'd keep using the AI thing now and then to check a regulation or plan meals on a budget. And I'd put in for the team leader job when it comes up in spring, because that's real money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ordinary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Plan meals on a budget? Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I type in what's in the fridge and what we've got to spend, and it gives me five dinners. Half of them the kids won't eat, but it saves me twenty minutes on a Sunday. That's about as far as I go with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the team leader job worth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two and a half thousand a year more. I've been passed over once. This time I'd go in with my numbers, how many connections I've done with no call-backs.

S0.say: She'd say fair enough, the useful bits stay and the rest goes quiet, and joke in the crew chat about tablets not working in the rain. Nothing dramatic.
S0.think: Privately it's a relief for both her and her partner, whose delivery job would have been at risk too. But it doesn't fix the money; they'd still be a fortnight from the edge.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, using AI occasionally to check regulations and plan budget meals. Applies for the spring team leader role worth about two and a half thousand a year, armed with her no-call-back record.
S0.quote: Half of them the kids won't eat, but it saves me twenty minutes on a Sunday.
S0.fieldNote: Beth thinks as a household, weighing her partner's van job alongside her own. She's practical and numbers-minded, ready to argue her case for promotion with data. Her AI use is modest and domestic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one's more likely, I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that we should get ahead of it and ask what training's coming. With friends I'd say it's Sam's job I'd worry about more than mine. I wouldn't post much online; it's not my style.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my side's fairly safe for a while. Brookfield keeps building, and every heat pump needs a bigger supply. It's the routing software and the van side, Sam's job, that I'd lie awake about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the other crews had used the new design software for a few months, I'd put my hand up to learn it. I'd set up a savings pot and put thirty a week in, and I'd sit down with Sam about whether he should start looking at other work now, while things are calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mainly for Sam. For me, more like a background hum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the software after others had. What makes you wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've seen the first version of everything be rubbish. The first tablet we had lost a week of job sheets. Let someone else find the bugs, then I'll be good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sam say if you raised other work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say he likes his van and his route and his radio. He's more stubborn than me. I'd probably leave a leaflet for the bus driver training on the table and see what happens.

S1.say: She'd say at work that the crew should get ahead of it and ask what training is coming. With friends she'd say she worries more about her partner's job than her own.
S1.think: She thinks her side is fairly safe for a while because Brookfield keeps building and heat pumps need bigger supplies. It's her partner's van work she'd lie awake about.
S1.do: Learns the new design software after other crews have used it a few months and saves thirty a week. Raises the idea of other work with her partner while things are calm.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mainly for her partner, with only a background hum for herself.
S1.quote: I'd probably leave a leaflet for the bus driver training on the table and see what happens.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry is about the household, and she sees her partner as more exposed than herself. She'd adopt new tools once proven, citing a tablet that lost a week of job sheets. Her nudging approach with her partner is gentle and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Both of us, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's be sensible and find out what the company's plan is before we panic. With friends I'd be more honest and say this one scares me. Online I'd probably share some news and keep my opinions to myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's both of us at once. If robots can drive the van and fit the cut-out, we've got two incomes going at the same time and about two weeks of savings. That's the bit that makes my stomach drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd go through every bill line by line and cut anything that isn't the mortgage, food or heat. I'd talk to my sister about whether we could move nearer her and sell the house before the market falls. And I'd find out exactly what government support there is, because pride doesn't pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be the one awake at three doing the spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell work to be sensible but tell friends it scares you. Which one's true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. At work you keep a level head because the young ones look at you. At home I'd be crying in the bath. That's just how it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Amira and Zain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we might move closer to Auntie Rania and they'd get a bigger garden. Try and make it sound like an adventure. Amira's thirteen, she'd see straight through it.

S2.say: She'd tell the crew to be sensible and find out the company's plan before panicking. With friends she'd admit this one scares her, and online she'd share news without opinions.
S2.think: Privately it hits both incomes at once: robots driving the van and fitting the cut-out, with two weeks of savings. That's what makes her stomach drop.
S2.do: Goes through every bill in the first month and cuts everything except mortgage, food and heat. Talks with her sister about selling and moving nearer before the market falls, and checks what government support exists.
S2.feel: Alarmed; she'd be awake at three doing the spreadsheet.
S2.quote: At work you keep a level head because the young ones look at you. At home I'd be crying in the bath.
S2.fieldNote: The double exposure of both earners drives her alarm. Her public calm and private distress are openly acknowledged, and she sees no contradiction. She'd take government help without embarrassment, which fits her pragmatic outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. A bit more room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work we've got a few years to get the training in, so let's ask for it now. I'd tell friends it's worrying but there's time to plan. I'd probably vote for whoever had the most sensible plan, not the loudest one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years is enough for me to do something. I've always thought I'd be good at teaching apprentices, and someone's going to need to train people on the robots for a while. Sam has time to retrain too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the trainer role at the technical college or the company training centre in the first year, and take the teaching certificate in the evenings. I'd keep the thirty a week going, more if I could. And I'd get Sam onto a course, maybe the bus licence, so we're not both in the same boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but organised. I like having a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't the robots need fewer trainers over time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably. It's not forever. It's a bridge, a few years of decent money while we work out what's next. I'm not looking for forever, I'm looking for the next five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you nudged Sam with a leaflet. Would you push harder here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Five years means there's no excuse. I'd sit him down properly with the numbers. He listens to numbers more than to me.

S3.say: She'd tell the crew there are a few years to get training in, so ask for it now. She'd vote for whoever has the most sensible plan, not the loudest one.
S3.think: She thinks five years is enough to act, perhaps teaching apprentices or training people on robots for a while. Her partner would also have time to retrain.
S3.do: Applies for a trainer role at the technical college or company training centre in year one and takes a teaching certificate in the evenings. Keeps saving thirty a week and sits her partner down with the numbers to get him onto a bus licence course.
S3.feel: Anxious but organised; she likes having a list.
S3.quote: I'm not looking for forever, I'm looking for the next five years.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives her a workable bridge plan, and she's clear it's temporary. She'd push her partner harder when there's no excuse for delay. Her politics are about competence, not ideology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. The kids would be nearly grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this right and there's no reason for anyone to be caught out. At work I'd say get your training in while it's paid for. I'd probably be quite boring about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I can get the kids through school and pay the mortgage down a fair bit. I'd retrain properly instead of grabbing the first thing. It's the first one where I don't feel squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the teaching certificate slowly over two years and keep doing connections in the meantime. I'd talk to Amira about her options, since she'd be choosing what to study right as it all lands. And I'd build the savings up to three months, which we've never had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, but mostly calm. It feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three months' savings, which you've never had. How would you get there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. The team leader money if I get it, no holidays abroad, Sam doing overtime in the Christmas rush. It'd take maybe four years, but ten years gives me four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Amira about what to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where people need a real person. Nursing, social work, maybe something technical with robots if she likes that. I'd tell her to keep her options open, which is what my mum told me and I ignored.

S4.say: She'd say there's time to do this right and no reason for anyone to be caught out. At work she'd tell people to get training in while it's paid for.
S4.think: Privately ten years means getting the kids through school, paying down the mortgage and retraining properly. It's the first picture where she doesn't feel squeezed.
S4.do: Takes the teaching certificate over two years while still doing connections. Talks with her daughter about what to study and builds savings toward three months over about four years.
S4.feel: A little uneasy but mostly calm; it feels manageable.
S4.quote: It'd take maybe four years, but ten years gives me four years.
S4.fieldNote: The decade gives her the slack she's never had, and she'd use it to build savings for the first time. Her worry moves to her daughter's choices. She describes her own approach as boring, which suits her steady style.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes both of us out at once. What would help is clear information from the company about timing, paid retraining for both of us, and some support to stop people losing their homes while they change jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You asked about me, but it's never just me. Every house on our street has two jobs in it. If you only look at one, you miss half of it.

headlineQuote: Every house on our street has two jobs in it. If you only look at one, you miss half of it.
portrait: Beth Rahman is a 43-year-old new connections lineworker in a booming commuter town, married to a delivery van driver, with two kids and about a fortnight of savings. She's tidy, numbers-minded and adopts new tools once they're proven. She thinks of risk as a household, and worries more about her partner's job than her own in milder change. The two-year AGI picture alarms her because both incomes go at once, while five years gives her a trainer role as a bridge and ten years finally lets her build savings. She keeps a level head at work and saves her fear for home.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would take both her and her partner's incomes at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Clear timing from the company, paid retraining for both of them, and support to stop families losing their homes while they change jobs.
